nodes.name: Persistent homology with torsion
nodes.statement: The extension of the theory of Persistent Homology to the case of persistent homology groups with torsion is an important open problem.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Extending persistent homology theory to persistent homology groups with torsion is open.

nodes.name: Robotic grasp space with torsion
nodes.statement: Let us assume that the cost of the grasp is given by the value $\varphi_\mathcal{G}(\{p,q\})=-\|p-q\|$, so relating the cost of a grasp to the level of closure of the robotic hand. For the sake of simplicity, let us examine the case $\mathcal{S}=S^2=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3:x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}$. In this case, the group ${H}_1^{(\mathcal{G},\varphi_\mathcal{G})}(u,v)$ has torsion, when $u<v<0$ and $u$ is close enough to zero. Indeed, we can consider the continuous function $f$ taking each unordered pair $\{p,q\}\in \mathcal{G}_v$ to the direction of the line $l$ through $p$ and $q$ (note that $\{p,q\}\in \mathcal{G}_v$ implies $p\neq q$, so that $l$ is well-defined). This direction can be seen as a point in the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$. Let us observe that, for $v$ close enough to zero, the function $f:\mathcal{G}_v\to \mathbb{RP}^2$ is a homotopy equivalence (the homotopy inverse of $f$ is the function $g:\mathbb{RP}^2\to \mathcal{G}_v$ that takes each direction $w$ to the unordered pair $\{p,q\}$, where $p$ and $q$ are the points at which the line through $(0,0,0)$, having direction $w$, meets $S^2$). Hence $f$ induces an isomorphism between the singular homology groups of $\mathcal{G}_v$ and $\mathbb{RP}^2$. As a consequence, since $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)$ has torsion, the persistent homology group ${H}_1^{(\mathcal{G},\varphi_\mathcal{G})}(u,v)$ has torsion, too, when $u$ is close enough to zero.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: For two-finger grasps of $S^2$ with cost $-\|p-q\|$, the sublevel sets are homotopy equivalent to $\mathbb{RP}^2$, so $H_1$ persistent groups have torsion.

nodes.name: Filtering function
nodes.statement: Filtrations are usually expressed by real functions $\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}$ called {\em filtering functions}.
nodes.section: Multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Stability of persistence diagrams
nodes.statement: The problem of stability in persistent homology has been studied by Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner and Harer in \cite{CoEdHa07} for scalar filtering functions. By using a descriptor called a \emph{persistence diagram}, they prove that persistent Betti numbers are stable under perturbations of filtering functions with respect to the max-norm, provided that the considered filtering functions are \emph{tame}.
nodes.section: Prior works
nodes.statement_short: Persistent Betti numbers of tame scalar filtering functions are stable under max-norm perturbations.
conclusions: persistent Betti numbers are stable under perturbations of filtering functions with respect to the max-norm

nodes.name: Partial orders $\preceq$ and $\prec$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: In this paper, the following relations $\preceq$ and $\prec$ are defined in $\mathbb{R}^n$: for $\vec u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)$ and $\vec v=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$, we say $\vec u\preceq\vec v$ (resp. $\vec u\prec\vec v$) if and only if $u_i\leq\ v_i$ (resp. $u_i<v_i$) for every index $i=1,\dots,n$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Max-norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Moreover, $\mathbb{R}^n$ is endowed with the usual $\max$-norm: $\left\|(u_1,u_2,\dots,u_n)\right\|_{\infty}=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|u_i|$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Set $\Delta^+$
nodes.statement: We shall use the following notations: $\Delta^+$ will be the open set $\{(\vec u,\vec v)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n:\vec u\prec\vec v\}$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Sublevel set $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec u\rangle$
nodes.statement: For every $n$-tuple $\vec u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and for every function $\vec\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}^n$, we shall denote by $X\langle\vec \varphi\preceq \vec u\,\rangle$ the set $\{x\in X:\varphi_i(x)\leq u_i,\ i=1,\dots,n\}$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Max-norm of a continuous function
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a compact topological space and $\vec\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is a continuous function, we shall set $\|\vec \varphi\|_\infty=\max_{x\in X}\|\vec \varphi(x)\|_\infty$.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence

nodes.name: Multidimensional persistent homology group
nodes.statement: Let $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Let $X$ be a topological space, and $\vec \varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}^n$ a continuous function. Let $i_*:{H}_k(X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec u\rangle)\rightarrow {H}_k(X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec v\rangle)$ be the homomorphism induced by the inclusion map $i:X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec u\rangle\hookrightarrow X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq\vec v\rangle$ with $\vec u\preceq\vec v$, where ${H}_k$ denotes the $k$th homology group with coefficients in an Abelian group $G$. If $\vec u\prec\vec v$, the image of $i_*$ is called the {\em multidimensional $k$th persistent homology group of $(X,\vec\varphi)$ at $(\vec u, \vec v)$}. We shall denote it by the symbol ${H}_k^{(X,\vec\varphi)}(\vec u, \vec v)$. The function ${H}_k^{(X,\vec\varphi)}$ is called the {\em multidimensional $k$th persistent homology group of $(X,\vec\varphi)$}.
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence
nodes.statement_short: The image in $H_k$ of the inclusion of the sublevel set at $\vec u$ into the one at $\vec v$, with coefficients in an Abelian group $G$.
nodes.label: PersHom

nodes.name: Choice of homology theory
nodes.statement: The choice of the particular homology we use is not essential in this context, in the sense that the results proven in this paper do not depend on this choice. However, while we will not further discuss this point, we recall that some important properties of persistent homology groups depend on the homology that is considered. As an example, the use of \v{C}ech homology with real coefficients allows us to assume that the function $\beta_\varphi:\Delta^+\to \mathbb{N}\cup \{\infty\}$ that takes each pair $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$ to the rank of the multidimensional $k$th persistent homology group of $(X,\vec\varphi)$ at $(\vec u, \vec v)$, is right-continuous in both its variables (cf. \cite{CeDiFeFrLa09}).
nodes.section: 1 Some definitions and properties in multidimensional persistence
nodes.statement_short: Results do not depend on the homology theory; with \v{C}ech homology the rank function is right-continuous.
nodes.label: rem_hom

nodes.name: Persistent homology groups on $\mathbb{RP}^2$ and $S^2$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{RP}^2$ be the real projective plane, represented by the unordered pairs $\{p,-p\}$ of opposite points of $S^2=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3:x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}$. Let us consider the filtering functions $\varphi,\psi:\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, defined by setting $\varphi(\{(x,y,z),-(x,y,z)\})=|z|$ and $\psi(\{(x,y,z),-(x,y,z)\})=2|z|$. Let us also consider the filtering function $\chi:S^2\to\mathbb{R}$, defined by setting $\chi(x,y,z)=|z|$. For each $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$, the persistent homology groups in degree $1$ computed at $(u,v)$ of $\varphi$, $\chi$ and $\psi$ are displayed in Figure~\ref{groups}, from left to right. The coefficients of the homology are taken in $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.statement_short: Degree-1 integer persistent homology groups of $|z|$, $2|z|$ on $\mathbb{RP}^2$ and $|z|$ on $S^2$.

nodes.name: Collection $Ab$ of Abelian groups
nodes.statement: In the following, $Ab$ will represent the collection of all Abelian groups, considered up to isomorphisms.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability

nodes.name: Pseudo-distance $d_T$
nodes.statement: Let $X$, $Y$ be two topological spaces, and $\vec\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}^n$, $\vec\psi:Y\to\mathbb{R}^n$ two continuous filtering functions. Let $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k:\Delta^+\to Ab$ and $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k:\Delta^+\to Ab$ the multidimensional persistent $k$-homology groups associated with the pairs $(X,\vec\varphi)$ and $(Y,\vec\psi)$, respectively. We assume that the homology coefficients are taken in an Abelian group. Let us consider the set $E$ of all $\epsilon\ge 0$ such that, setting $\vec\epsilon=(\epsilon,\ldots,\epsilon)\in \mathbb{R}^n$, the following statements hold for each $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$: \begin{enumerate} \item a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)\}$ exists; \item a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)\}$ exists. \end{enumerate} We define $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)$ equal to $\inf E$ if $E$ is not empty, and equal to $\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: $d_T$ is the infimum of $\epsilon\ge0$ such that each group at $(\vec u,\vec v)$ has a subgroup surjecting onto the other's group at $(\vec u-\vec\epsilon,\vec v+\vec\epsilon)$, both ways.
nodes.label: distancedef

nodes.name: Pseudo-distance
nodes.statement: Before proceeding, we recall that the term ``pseudo-distance'' means that the considered function verifies all the properties of a distance, with the possible exception of the one assuring that two elements having a vanishing distance must coincide.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability

nodes.name: Extended (pseudo-distance)
nodes.statement: The term ``extended'' refers to the possibility that the function takes the value $\infty$.

nodes.name: $d_T$ is an extended pseudo-distance
nodes.statement: The function $d_T$ is an extended pseudo-distance.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
conclusions: The function $d_T$ is an extended pseudo-distance.
nodes.label: isapseudodistance

nodes.name: Proof that $d_T$ is an extended pseudo-distance
nodes.statement: The following statements hold: \begin{description} \item[$i)$] $d_T$ is non-negative by definition; \item[$ii)$]The equality $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k\right)=0$ is obtained by taking $\epsilon=0$ and considering the identical homomorphism $id: H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)\to H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$; \item[$iii)$]$d_T$ is symmetrical by definition; \item[$iv)$]Assume that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)=\epsilon_1$ and $d_T\left( H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)=\epsilon_2$. Let $\eta$ be an arbitrarily small positive real number. The definition of $d_T$ implies that for each $(\vec u,\vec v)\in \Delta^+$ a surjective homomorphism $f$ from a subgroup $F$ of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta))$, and a surjective homomorphism $g$ from a subgroup $G$ of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta))$ onto $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$ exist. Now, we can consider the subgroup $\tilde{F}=f^{-1}(G)\subseteq H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$. Obviously, the function $g_{|G}\circ f_{|\tilde{F}}$ is a surjective homomorphism from the subgroup $\tilde{F}$ of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$. Analogously, we can construct a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u-(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)-(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta),\vec v+(\vec \epsilon_1+\vec\eta)+(\vec \epsilon_2+\vec\eta))$. This implies that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)\le\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+2\eta$. Since $\eta$ can be taken arbitrarily small, it follows that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Z,\vec\chi)}_k\right)\le\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2$, so proving the triangle inequality for $d_T$. \end{description}
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Direct verification of the pseudo-distance axioms; the triangle inequality composes the restricted surjective homomorphisms.

nodes.name: $d_T$ between the groups of Figure 1
nodes.statement: As a simple example, we can easily check that $d_T$ takes the value $1$ between the first two persistent homology groups represented in Figure~\ref{groups}, and the value $\infty$ between the first and the third and between the second and the third persistent homology groups represented in the same figure.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: $d_T$ is $1$ between the two $\mathbb{RP}^2$ examples and $\infty$ between either of them and the $S^2$ example.

nodes.name: $d_T$ is not a distance
nodes.statement: We observe that the pseudo-distance $d_T$ is not a distance. For example, we can consider the two Abelian groups $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$ (obtained by adding infinite copies of the integer numbers) and $\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$. We can find two topological spaces $X$, $Y$ such that their homology groups in degree $1$ are these two groups, respectively. If we take the two filtering functions $\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}$, $\psi:Y\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\varphi\equiv\psi\equiv 0$, we have that $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$ and $H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)= \mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}$ for any $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ with $u\ge 0$. Obviously, if $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ with $u< 0$ we get that both $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ and $H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ are the trivial group. In any case, it is easy to find a surjective homomorphism from $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ and a surjective homomorphism from $H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, so that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)=0$. However, the groups $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v), H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ are not isomorphic, for $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ with $u\ge 0$.
nodes.section: 2 The pseudo-distance $d_T$ and the proof of its stability
nodes.statement_short: Constant filtrations on spaces with $H_1=\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}$ give $d_T=0$ for non-isomorphic groups.
nodes.label: rem_pd

nodes.name: Persistence diagram representation for field coefficients
nodes.statement: Let us go back to the case of filtering functions taking values in $\mathbb{R}$. In this case, if the Abelian group $G$ of homology coefficients is also a field, it is well known that the persistent homology groups can be described by persistence diagrams, under the assumption that the topological space is triangulable (cf. \cite{CoEdHa07} for tame filtering functions, and \cite{CeDiFeFrLa09} for continuous filtering functions).

nodes.origin_citation: Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner, Harer 2007; Cerri et al. 2009
nodes.statement_short: With field coefficients and triangulable spaces, scalar persistent homology groups are described by persistence diagrams.
assumptions: the Abelian group $G$ of homology coefficients is also a field
conclusions: the persistent homology groups can be described by persistence diagrams

nodes.name: Persistence diagram
nodes.statement: In plain words, the persistence diagram is the collection of all points $(u,v)$ where $u$ and $v$ represent the ``birth'' and ``death'' of a homology class, varying the sub-level sets of the topological space $X$ with respect to the filtering function $\varphi:X\to \mathbb{R}$. Each one of these pairs $(u,v)$ is endowed with a multiplicity. By definition, all the pairs $(u,u)$ belong to the persistent diagram, each of them counted with infinite multiplicity.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner, Harer 2007; Cerri et al. 2009
nodes.statement_short: Multiset of birth-death pairs $(u,v)$ of homology classes of sublevel sets, plus the diagonal with infinite multiplicity.

nodes.name: Matching distance $d_{match}$
nodes.statement: The matching distance $d_{match}$ between two persistence diagrams is the infimum of the cost of a matching (i.e. a bijective correspondence) between two persistence diagrams.
nodes.section: 2.1 Relationship between $d_T$ and $d_{match}$ in the $1$-dimensional case, if there is no torsion

nodes.genus: the infimum of the cost of a matching

nodes.name: Cost of a matching
nodes.statement: The cost of a matching $f$ is defined to be the maximum displacement of the points of the persistence diagrams, induced by $f$. Each displacement is measured by the max-norm on the real plane.

nodes.name: $d_T$ is bounded by the matching distance
nodes.statement: Let $X,Y$ be two triangulable spaces endowed with two continuous functions $\varphi: X \to \mathbb{R}$, $\psi: Y \to \mathbb{R}$. Let us consider the persistent homology groups $H^{(X,\varphi)}_k$, $H^{(Y,\varphi)}_k$ with homology coefficients in a field. Let $D_\varphi$ and $D_\psi$ be the persistent diagrams associated with the filtering functions $\varphi$ and $\psi$, respectively. Then, for any integer $k$, $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)\le d_{match}(D_\varphi,D_\psi)$.

nodes.name: Proof of $d_T\le d_{match}$
nodes.statement: Since the coefficients are taken in a field, our persistent homology groups have no torsion, and they can be described by their persistent Betti numbers functions $\beta_\varphi$, $\beta_\psi$, where we set $\beta_\varphi(u,v)=\dim {H}_k^{(X,\varphi)}(u, v)$, $\beta_\psi(u,v)=\dim {H}_k^{(Y,\psi)}(u, v)$, for $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$. Obviously, for each $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, we have different persistent Betti numbers functions $\beta_\varphi$ of $\varphi$ (which should be denoted $\beta_{\varphi,k}$, say) but, for the sake of notational simplicity, we omit adding any reference to $k$. Let us assume that the matching distance $d_{match}$ between our persistence diagrams takes the value $\bar \lambda$. Then, from the Representation Theorem 2.17 in \cite{CeDiFeFrLa09} (cf. also the \emph{$k$-triangle Lemma} in \cite{CoEdHa07}), it follows that for every $\lambda>\bar\lambda$ and every pair $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ the inequalities $\beta_\varphi(u-\lambda,v+ \lambda)\leq\beta_\psi(u,v)$ and $\beta_\psi(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\leq\beta_\varphi(u,v)$ hold. This fact immediately implies that for each $(u,v)\in \Delta^+$ \begin{enumerate} \item a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\}$ exists; \item a surjective homomorphism from a subgroup of $ H^{(Y,\psi)}_k(u,v)$ onto $ H^{(X,\varphi)}_k(u-\lambda,v+\lambda)\}$ exists. \end{enumerate} Hence $d_T\left( H^{(X,\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\psi)}_k\right)\le\lambda$ for any $\lambda>\bar\lambda$. This implies our thesis.

nodes.name: Proof of the homeomorphism lemma
nodes.statement: The homeomorphism $h$ induces a chain isomorphism $h_*$. Obviously, $h_*$ takes cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries. Let us consider the set $S$ of the elements of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$ that contain at least one cycle whose image by $h_*$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. We claim that $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$. Indeed, if $a_1,a_2\in S$ then two cycles $\gamma_1\in a_1$, $\gamma_2\in a_2$ exist, such that $h_*(\gamma_1), h_*(\gamma_2)$ are cycles in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(\gamma_1)+h_*(\gamma_2)=h_*(\gamma_1+\gamma_2)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too. Since $\gamma_1+\gamma_2\in a_1+a_2$, it follows that the equivalence class $a_1+a_2$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the sum. Furthermore, if $a\in S$ then a cycle $\gamma\in a$ exists, such that $h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(-\gamma)=-h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too. Since $-\gamma\in -a$, it follows that the equivalence class $-a$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the computation of the opposite. In summary, $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$. Now, let us define the homomorphism $f:S\to H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$. In the following, for each $a\in S$, let us fix a cycle $\gamma_a\in a$ such that $h_*(\gamma_a)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec \epsilon\rangle$. For every $a\in S$ we define $f(a)$ as the element of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$ that contains $h_*(\gamma_a)$ (i.e., in symbols, $[h_*(\gamma_a)]$). We claim that $f$ is a homomorphism. In order to do that, let us consider three elements $a_1,a_2,a\in H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, such that $a_1+a_2=a$. Obviously, $$f(a_1)+f(a_2)=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})]+[h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})+h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]$$ $$f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})].$$ Now, $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]-[h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})-h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_{a})]$. Since $a_1+a_2=a$, a $(k+1)$-cycle $\tau$ in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$ exists, such that $\partial \tau=\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $h_*(\tau)$ is a $(k+1)$-cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Moreover, recalling that $h_*$ is a chain map, $\partial h_*(\tau)=h_*(\partial \tau)=h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$, so that $h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$ is a boundary in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$ and hence $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)]$ is the null element in $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$. This proves that $f(a_1)+f(a_2)=f(a)$. Finally, we claim that $f$ is surjective. Indeed, let $b\in H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$ and $\beta\in b$, so that $\beta$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Let $\alpha$ be the cycle $\left((h_*)^{-1}\right)(\beta)=\left(h^{-1}\right)^*(\beta)$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi\circ h^{-1}-\vec\psi\|_\infty=\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $\alpha$ is a cycle in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec u\rangle$. Therefore the element $a\in H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ the cycle $\alpha$ belongs to is an element of the set $S$. Then $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})]$. Now, $\gamma_{a}$ and $\alpha$ are homologous in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$. Once again because of the inequality $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, it follows that $h_*(\gamma_{a})$ and $\beta=h_*(\alpha)$ are homologous in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence $f(a)=b$, and $f$ is proven to be surjective.

nodes.name: Sum of cycles
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $a_1,a_2\in S$ then two cycles $\gamma_1\in a_1$, $\gamma_2\in a_2$ exist, such that $h_*(\gamma_1), h_*(\gamma_2)$ are cycles in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(\gamma_1)+h_*(\gamma_2)=h_*(\gamma_1+\gamma_2)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too.
nodes.statement_short: $h_*$ of a sum of cycles lies in the sublevel set
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Closure under sum
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma_1+\gamma_2\in a_1+a_2$, it follows that the equivalence class $a_1+a_2$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the sum.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $a_1+a_2\in S$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Closure under opposite
nodes.statement: Furthermore, if $a\in S$ then a cycle $\gamma\in a$ exists, such that $h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence the cycle $h_*(-\gamma)=-h_*(\gamma)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$, too. Since $-\gamma\in -a$, it follows that the equivalence class $-a$ belongs to $S$. That means that $S$ is closed with respect to the computation of the opposite.
nodes.statement_short: $S$ is closed under negation
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: $S$ is a subgroup
nodes.statement: In summary, $S$ is a subgroup of $ H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(\vec u,\vec v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $S$ is a subgroup
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Define $f$
nodes.statement: Now, let us define the homomorphism $f:S\to H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$. In the following, for each $a\in S$, let us fix a cycle $\gamma_a\in a$ such that $h_*(\gamma_a)$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec \epsilon\rangle$. For every $a\in S$ we define $f(a)$ as the element of $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(\vec u-\vec \epsilon,\vec v+\vec \epsilon)$ that contains $h_*(\gamma_a)$ (i.e., in symbols, $[h_*(\gamma_a)]$).
nodes.statement_short: Define $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_a)]$ via fixed representatives
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: $f$ is a homomorphism
nodes.statement: We claim that $f$ is a homomorphism. In order to do that, let us consider three elements $a_1,a_2,a\in H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, such that $a_1+a_2=a$. Obviously, $$f(a_1)+f(a_2)=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})]+[h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})+h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]$$ $$f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})].$$ Now, $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]-[h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})-h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_{a})]$. Since $a_1+a_2=a$, a $(k+1)$-cycle $\tau$ in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$ exists, such that $\partial \tau=\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $h_*(\tau)$ is a $(k+1)$-cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Moreover, recalling that $h_*$ is a chain map, $\partial h_*(\tau)=h_*(\partial \tau)=h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$, so that $h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$ is a boundary in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$ and hence $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)]$ is the null element in $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$. This proves that $f(a_1)+f(a_2)=f(a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $f$ is a homomorphism
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Express $f$ on a sum
nodes.statement: In order to do that, let us consider three elements $a_1,a_2,a\in H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$, such that $a_1+a_2=a$. Obviously, $$f(a_1)+f(a_2)=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})]+[h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1})+h_*(\gamma_{a_2})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]$$ $$f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})].$$
nodes.statement_short: Write $f(a_1)+f(a_2)$ and $f(a)$ via representatives
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Difference
nodes.statement: Now, $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})]-[h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2})-h_*(\gamma_{a})]=[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_{a})]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the class of $h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Bounding chain $\tau$
nodes.statement: Since $a_1+a_2=a$, a $(k+1)$-cycle $\tau$ in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$ exists, such that $\partial \tau=\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a$.
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $\tau$ with $\partial\tau=\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Image is a boundary
nodes.statement: Given that $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $h_*(\tau)$ is a $(k+1)$-cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Moreover, recalling that $h_*$ is a chain map, $\partial h_*(\tau)=h_*(\partial \tau)=h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$, so that $h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)$ is a boundary in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$ and hence $[h_*(\gamma_{a_1}+\gamma_{a_2}-\gamma_a)]$ is the null element in $ H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$. This proves that $f(a_1)+f(a_2)=f(a)$.
nodes.statement_short: $h_*(\tau)$ lies in the shifted sublevel set, so the difference is null
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: $f$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Finally, we claim that $f$ is surjective. Indeed, let $b\in H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$ and $\beta\in b$, so that $\beta$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Let $\alpha$ be the cycle $\left((h_*)^{-1}\right)(\beta)=\left(h^{-1}\right)^*(\beta)$. Given that $\|\vec\varphi\circ h^{-1}-\vec\psi\|_\infty=\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $\alpha$ is a cycle in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec u\rangle$. Therefore the element $a\in H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ the cycle $\alpha$ belongs to is an element of the set $S$. Then $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})]$. Now, $\gamma_{a}$ and $\alpha$ are homologous in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$. Once again because of the inequality $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, it follows that $h_*(\gamma_{a})$ and $\beta=h_*(\alpha)$ are homologous in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Hence $f(a)=b$, and $f$ is proven to be surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Show $f$ is surjective via $h^{-1}$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Preimage cycle
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $b\in H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k(u-\epsilon,v+\epsilon)$ and $\beta\in b$, so that $\beta$ is a cycle in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec u-\vec\epsilon\rangle$. Let $\alpha$ be the cycle $\left((h_*)^{-1}\right)(\beta)=\left(h^{-1}\right)^*(\beta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $b$, $\beta\in b$ and $\alpha=(h^{-1})_*\beta$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: $\alpha$ in sublevel set
nodes.statement: Given that $\|\vec\varphi\circ h^{-1}-\vec\psi\|_\infty=\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, $\alpha$ is a cycle in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec u\rangle$. Therefore the element $a\in H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k(u,v)$ the cycle $\alpha$ belongs to is an element of the set $S$. Then $f(a)=[h_*(\gamma_{a})]$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha$ lies in the sublevel set at $\vec u$, so its class is in $S$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Homologous images
nodes.statement: Now, $\gamma_{a}$ and $\alpha$ are homologous in $X\langle\vec\varphi\preceq \vec v\rangle$. Once again because of the inequality $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h\|_\infty\le \epsilon$, it follows that $h_*(\gamma_{a})$ and $\beta=h_*(\alpha)$ are homologous in $Y\langle\vec\psi\preceq \vec v+\vec\epsilon\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Images of homologous cycles remain homologous after the shift
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Conclude surjectivity
nodes.statement: Hence $f(a)=b$, and $f$ is proven to be surjective.
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Near-optimal homeomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let us set $\bar \delta=\delta\left((X,\vec\varphi),(Y,\vec\psi)\right)$. Because of the definition of natural pseudodistance, for each $\eta>0$ we can find a homeomorphism $h_\eta:X\to Y$ such that $\|\vec \varphi-\vec \psi\circ h_\eta\|_\infty\le \bar\delta+\eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $h_\eta$ with $\|\vec\varphi-\vec\psi\circ h_\eta\|_\infty\le\bar\delta+\eta$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement: By applying Lemma \ref{lemmahom} to both the homeomorphisms $h_\eta:X\to Y$ and $h_\eta^{-1}:Y\to X$, we get that $d_T\left( H^{(X,\vec\varphi)}_k, H^{(Y,\vec\psi)}_k\right)\le \bar\delta+\eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.7 for $h_\eta$ and $h_\eta^{-1}$ gives $d_T\le\bar\delta+\eta$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$

nodes.name: Let $\eta\to0$
nodes.statement: Since $\eta$ can be chosen arbitrarily close to $0$, our thesis follows.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by letting $\eta\to0$
nodes.section: 2.2 Stability of the pseudo-distance $d_T$
